claims.claim: ANSI/NISO Z39.18 makes a summary a required component of a scientific or technical report and defines its content as the problem under investigation, the principal results and conclusions, and a recommended course of action for decision makers.

Under the same standard the summary introduces no new information yet is independent from the user's point of view, with all symbols, abbreviations, and acronyms defined and no cross-references; a separate executive summary for a management-level audience is often prepared when a print report exceeds 50 pages, and should not exceed 10 pages.

Z39.18 requires a 'Methods, Assumptions, and Procedures' section complete enough that a knowledgeable reader could duplicate the investigation, and requires the system of measurement to be identified there; the standard's preferred unit standard is the International System of Units.

Z39.18 states that graphs show relationships among data, directs that units of measurement be indicated in a table's title, column heads, or a note, requires a key or caption definition for symbols appearing in a figure but not in the text, and advises grid lines or, better, a table when highly accurate readings are needed.

Z39.18 requires a list of symbols, abbreviations, and acronyms when more than five appear that are not readily recognised as standard in the field, and directs that in a report with extensive notation all equations be displayed and numbered, with symbols defined below the formula.

The NASA Systems Engineering Handbook fixes the modal-verb convention (shall = requirement, will = facts or declaration of purpose, should = goal), puts personnel requirements in the form 'responsible party shall perform such and such' and directs the use of the active rather than the passive voice, asks for one thought per requirement statement with one subject and one predicate, requires tolerances with performance values, and rules out ambiguous terms such as 'as appropriate', 'etc.', 'and/or', and 'but not limited to'.

The same handbook's requirements validation checklist asks explicitly whether all assumptions have been stated, includes identifying entry and success criteria for technical reviews within technical planning, and gives a decision report template whose first section is a half-page executive summary carrying a one-sentence recommendation and a one-sentence problem statement, and which reserves a section for documenting dissent and how it was addressed.

The Rogers Commission found that in the January 27, 1986 meetings the managers compared, as a function of temperature, the flights for which O-ring thermal distress had been observed, not the frequency of occurrence based on all flights, and that in that comparison nothing looked irregular between 53 F and 75 F.

Considering the entire flight history, the Commission reported three incidents of O-ring thermal distress out of twenty flights at O-ring temperatures of 66 F (18.9 C) or above, against thermal distress on all four flights at 63 F (17.2 C) or below, and concluded that a careful analysis of the flight history would have revealed the correlation of O-ring damage and low temperature, which neither NASA nor Thiokol had carried out.

The Commission also found the launch decision flawed because those who made it were unaware of the contractor's initial written recommendation against launching below 53 F (11.7 C) and of the continuing opposition of the Thiokol engineers after management reversed its position; Roger Boisjoly testified that when asked to quantify his concern he could not.

A peer-reviewed statistical analysis of the 23 pre-accident launches found strong statistical evidence of a temperature effect on O-ring thermal distress and estimated at least a 0.13 probability of catastrophic field-joint O-ring failure at the 31 F (-0.6 C) launch condition, against at least 0.02 had the flight been postponed to 60 F (15.6 C).

Reading Challenger as primarily a failure of graphical presentation is contested: Robison, Boisjoly, Hoeker, and Young argue the Thiokol engineers recommended against launch because the projected launch temperature was far outside their field database of successful launches, and because they had asked for but not received data needed to determine the cause of the previous January's massive blow-by.

The Columbia Accident Investigation Board reproduced a Debris Assessment Team briefing slide titled 'Review Of Test Data Indicates Conservatism for Tile Penetration' whose own text reads 'Volume of ramp is 1920cu in vs 3 cu in for test', wrote that as information gets passed up an organization hierarchy key explanations and supporting information are filtered out, and recorded the finding that the endemic use of PowerPoint briefing slides instead of technical papers illustrates problematic methods of technical communication at NASA.

The Crater model's test projectiles reached a maximum volume of 3 cubic inches (49.2 cm3) and outside its validated limits Crater's precision is unknown; the Board reported the slide's estimate as 640 times larger than the calibration data (1920 / 3 = 640, and 1920 in3 is 0.0315 m3 using the exact factor 1 in = 2.54E-02 m) and noted that later analysis put the debris object at about 400 times larger.

Edward Tufte's analysis of that slide, reproduced by the Board on the same page, records that 'significant' and 'significantly' appear five times on the slide with different de facto meanings and that the unit cubic inches is written three different ways.

Crowd-sourced experiments found that the subjective impact of y-axis truncation is persistent across visualization designs, even for designs with explicit visual cues that truncation has taken place; the same authors show truncation can be beneficial as well as harmful depending on communicative and analytic intent, and recommend scaling around the meaningful effect sizes and variation intended for communication.

The NSPE Code of Ethics requires engineers to be objective and truthful in professional reports, statements, or testimony, to include all relevant and pertinent information, and states that such material should bear the date indicating when it was current; it permits engineers to express technical opinions publicly that are founded upon knowledge of the facts and competence in the subject matter, and requires that credit for engineering work be given to those to whom it is due.

Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 34(a)(1)(A) allows a party to request production of designated documents or electronically stored information, including writings, drawings, graphs, charts, photographs, sound recordings, images, and other data or data compilations stored in any medium, which is why ordinary engineering email, tickets, and notebooks can become evidence.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How much of the Challenger launch decision is explained by how the O-ring data were presented
positions: The Rogers Commission recorded that only the flights showing thermal distress were compared against temperature, and concluded a careful analysis of the whole flight history would have revealed the correlation with low temperature. That is a finding about the analysis and its presentation.

Dalal, Fowlkes, and Hoadley demonstrated that the full 23-flight record carries strong statistical evidence of a temperature effect, so the information needed was available and recoverable at the time.

Robison, Boisjoly, Hoeker, and Young argue the engineers did what they were professionally obliged to do: they recommended against launch because the projected temperature lay far outside their field database, and they lacked data they had formally requested. On this reading the decisive failure was in the review and management process rather than in the engineers' charts.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states what the Commission and the later statistical work establish, that the incident-only comparison hid a pattern the full record contains, and says explicitly that scholarship disputes the stronger claim that better charts alone would have changed the outcome. The lesson also carries the Commission's separate finding that the decision-makers were unaware of the written recommendation at all. The professional-conduct dimension is handed to engineering-ethics.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether truncating a chart axis is always dishonest
positions: Truncation reliably inflates perceived effect size, and explicit warning cues in the design do not neutralize it.
The same authors present cases where truncation is beneficial and argue the scale should match the size of the effect and variation the author intends to communicate.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the rule as 'label the axis, make the baseline visible, and choose the scale around the effect that matters' rather than 'always start at zero', which is what the evidence actually supports.

conflictingEvidence.issue: By what factor the Columbia foam debris exceeded the Crater model's validated range
positions: The briefing slide's own numbers give 1920 cubic inches against 3 cubic inches for the test data, a factor of 640, and the Board's narrative states that one estimate of the debris was 640 times larger than the calibration data.

The Board also notes that later analysis showed the debris object was about 400 times larger, and elsewhere describes NASA as having accepted use of Crater to model a debris impact 400 times outside validated limits.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson gives both figures and attributes each: 640 is the ratio the slide's own numbers imply and the figure the Board's narrative uses for that estimate, 400 is the Board's later-analysis figure. Neither ratio appears on the slide itself, which is the point of the example.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft asserted nothing checkable about engineering communication. Its body was subject-agnostic boilerplate ('a concept students use to organize information') that no source supports and that could describe any topic in any subject.
The draft's toolbox-drawer and map-legend analogies did not describe engineering documents at all and were discarded.
The draft had no analogyLimits, no compareContrast, no real worked example, only four vocabulary terms, and three-option questions, none of which meet the schema.

An earlier unfinished worker draft at these paths cited the NASA Systems Engineering Handbook under a newly minted source id and a different URL from the one already in the phase-1 source registry; it also stated flatly that Z39.18 says to use a table when highly accurate readings are needed, and that the 640 ratio 'appears nowhere'. All three were corrected here.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the generated draft entirely with sourced material built on ANSI/NISO Z39.18, the NASA Systems Engineering Handbook, the Rogers Commission report, and the CAIB report.
Reused the existing registry source id nasa-se-handbook-sp-2016-6105-rev2 with its registered NTRS URL, rather than minting a second record for the same handbook.
Corrected the Z39.18 figure-versus-table guidance: the standard says to use grid lines, or better a table, when highly accurate readings are needed, rather than flatly mandating a table.

Attributed the 'significant' and 'cubic inches' criticisms of the Columbia slide to Edward Tufte's analysis as reproduced in CAIB Volume I, not to the Board's own findings; the Board's own words are the hierarchy-filtering passage and the PowerPoint finding.
Added the Board's statement of the 640 ratio and its later-analysis figure of about 400 times, so the lesson does not imply the ratio was never recorded anywhere.

Grounded the Challenger case in the Commission's own Chapter VI numbers rather than in a general claim that the charts were bad, and added the Chapter V finding that the decision-makers were unaware of the written recommendation.
Added the contested-scholarship caveat so the lesson does not adopt any single account of the charts, and handed the professional-conduct dimension to engineering-ethics.
Verified every number in the worked example with Bash before publication: 1920 / 3 = 640; 3 in3 = 49.2 cm3; 1920 in3 = 0.0315 m3; all Fahrenheit-to-Celsius conversions.
Handed significant figures and uncertainty arithmetic to the merged units topic instead of re-teaching them.
Added the required educational-material statement and the explicit note that this is not engineering design guidance and not legal advice.
rightsIssues: ANSI/NISO Z39.18 is copyrighted. Its own notice permits reproduction for noncommercial purposes provided it is reproduced accurately, the source is identified, and NISO copyright status is acknowledged. Nothing beyond short attributed phrases is reproduced here and the usage is recorded as REFERENCE_ONLY.
The NSPE Code of Ethics is copyrighted. Only short attributed phrases from Rules of Practice 3(a) and 3(b) and Professional Obligation 9 appear.

Dalal, Fowlkes and Hoadley (1989) and Robison et al. (2002) are paywalled journal articles used as REFERENCE_ONLY. The Dalal full text was read from an open university course copy and the Robison abstract from the PubMed record; the DOIs are registered as canonical.

The Debris Assessment Team slide quoted in the worked example is reproduced inside CAIB Volume I, a U.S. Government work. The quotation is limited to the slide's title line, one bullet fragment, and one numeric sub-bullet, all attributed. Edward Tufte's annotations printed on the same page are his own copyrighted analysis; they are summarised and attributed rather than reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Report of the Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident, Volume I (June 6, 1986)
sourceRecords.provider: Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident (NASA History Office electronic edition)
sourceRecords.license: Work of the United States Government; no copyright asserted on the electronic edition
sourceRecords.notes: Chapter V (v1ch5.htm) and Chapter VI (v1ch6.htm) fetched with curl and converted to text in this run. Chapter V opens 'The decision to launch the Challenger was flawed' (p. 82) and records that the decision-makers were unaware of the contractor's initial written recommendation against launch below 53 degrees Fahrenheit and of the engineers' continuing opposition after management reversed its position; it carries Boisjoly's testimony that when asked to quantify his concern he could not, and the exchange in which a 75-degree flight with blow-by was raised against his conclusion. Chapter VI ('Temperature Effects', pp. 143-148) supplies the data-presentation finding: managers 'compared as a function of temperature the flights for which thermal distress of O-rings had been observed-not the frequency of occurrence based on all flights (Figure 6)'; that in that view 'there is nothing irregular in the distribution' between 53 and 75 degrees Fahrenheit; that with all flights included (Figure 7) 'only three incidents of O-ring thermal distress occurred out of twenty flights with O-ring temperatures at 66 degrees Fahrenheit or above, whereas, all four flights with O-ring temperatures at 63 degrees Fahrenheit or below experienced O-ring thermal distress'; and finding 6, that 'A careful analysis of the flight history of O-ring performance would have revealed the correlation of O-ring damage and low temperature. Neither NASA nor Thiokol carried out such an analysis'. Facts synthesized; only short attributed phrases quoted.

sourceRecords.title: Columbia Accident Investigation Board Report, Volume I (August 2003)
sourceRecords.license: Work of the United States Government; no copyright asserted
sourceRecords.notes: 248-page PDF downloaded and text-extracted locally with pypdf in this run. Chapter 6 records that Crater 'predicts possible damage', that 'When used outside its validated limits, Crater's precision is unknown', and that the test projectiles were 'relatively small (maximum volume of 3 cubic inches)'; the Board's parameter table marks the STS-107 values for projectile diameter and velocity as outside validated limits. The 'Engineering by Viewgraphs' box on the page numbered 191 (PDF page 191 of 248) reproduces the Debris Assessment Team slide titled 'Review Of Test Data Indicates Conservatism for Tile Penetration', including the bullet 'Flight condition is significantly outside of test database' and the sub-bullet 'Volume of ramp is 1920cu in vs 3 cu in for test', together with Edward Tufte's annotations (five uses of 'significant'/'significantly' with different de facto meanings; 'cubic inches' written three different ways). The Board's own narrative on the same spread states that one estimate of the debris 'was 640 times larger than the data used to calibrate the model' and parenthetically that '(Later analysis showed that the debris object was actually 400 times larger)'; that 'As information gets passed up an organization hierarchy... key explanations and supporting information is filtered out'; and that 'The Board views the endemic use of PowerPoint briefing slides instead of technical papers as an illustration of the problematic methods of technical communication at NASA'. Chapter 7 also records the Naval Reactors practice of documenting contractor technical recommendations in peer-reviewed formal written correspondence rather than briefings, and of encouraging minority opinions. Only short attributed phrases quoted.

sourceRecords.title: Risk Analysis of the Space Shuttle: Pre-Challenger Prediction of Failure
sourceRecords.provider: Journal of the American Statistical Association 84(408): 945-957 (Dalal, Fowlkes and Hoadley)
sourceRecords.notes: Full text read in this run from an open university course copy (https://www.sfu.ca/~joanh/stat475-675/DalalEtAl_JASA1989.pdf), text-extracted with pypdf; the DOI record is registered as the canonical location. Abstract and Section 1 verified verbatim: using data from the 23 preaccident launches, 'analyses via binomial and binary logistic regression show that there is strong statistical evidence of a temperature effect on incidents of O-ring thermal distress'; 'a probabilistic risk assessment at 31 F, the temperature at which Challenger was launched, yields at least a 13% probability of catastrophic field-joint O-ring failure. Postponement to 60 F would have reduced the probability to at least 2%.' Figure 1 contrasts panel (a), the incident-only plot, with panel (b), captioned as including flights with no incidents. Used here only for the data-presentation point and the magnitude of the temperature effect; no prose adapted.

sourceRecords.title: Representation and misrepresentation: Tufte and the Morton Thiokol engineers on the Challenger
sourceRecords.provider: Science and Engineering Ethics 8(1): 59-81 (Robison, Boisjoly, Hoeker and Young)
sourceRecords.notes: Abstract and bibliographic record retrieved in this run from the NCBI E-utilities PubMed record (PMID 11840958); the full text is paywalled and was not read. Cited only for the position the paper takes: the authors, one of whom is Roger Boisjoly himself, examine Edward Tufte's analysis of the event and hold that the Morton Thiokol engineers 'recommended against the launch of Challenger because the projected launch temperature between 26 degrees F to 29 degrees F was far outside their field database of successful launches', that they 'had asked for, but not received, data necessary to determine the cause of massive blow-by on the launch the previous January', and that the engineers 'did what they were ethically as well as professionally obligated to do'. Used to prevent the lesson from overstating any single account of the charts.

sourceRecords.title: Truncating the Y-Axis: Threat or Menace?
sourceRecords.provider: Correll, Bertini and Franconeri; arXiv:1907.02035 (later published at ACM CHI 2020)
sourceRecords.license: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license (Nonexclusive-distrib 1.0) as shown on the abstract page
sourceRecords.notes: Abstract page fetched and read in this run. Supports: bar charts with y-axes that do not begin at zero can visually exaggerate effect sizes; the authors present examples where truncation is beneficial as well as harmful depending on communicative and analytic intent; their crowd-sourced experiments find that 'the subjective impact of axis truncation is persistent across visualizations designs, even for designs with explicit visual cues that indicate truncation has taken place'; and they suggest designers 'consider the scale of the meaningful effect sizes and variation they intend to communicate, regardless of the visual encoding'. Used both for the caution against truncation and for the honest caveat that a blanket always-start-at-zero rule overstates the evidence.

sourceRecords.notes: Official uscourts.gov PDF of the current rules downloaded and text-extracted with pypdf in this run, and cross-checked against the Cornell Legal Information Institute copy at https://www.law.cornell.edu/rules/frcp/rule_34. Used only to support the narrow claim that ordinary engineering working records are the kind of material a civil litigant can compel. The lesson gives no legal advice and says so.
